reasoning: ط is emphatic (T) and ح is 7. The long vowel is ii, and the taa marbuta after ن is e.

Feminine imperative of the loan verb shayyak 'to check', with the usual Levantine syncope (shayyki). It could also be said sheeki, so I am less sure of the vowelling. waatsaab is the normal local form of WhatsApp.
The dual of miyye is miiteen, with a long ee. khamsiin has a long ii. 'And' is a bare w after a vowel.
Standard kitaab with a long aa in the second syllable. Everyday word in Palestinian.
ق is a glottal stop and the shadda doubles d, giving 'addeesh. btaakhud is the masculine 2nd-person present; the b- prefix is attached as in bti7ki. Literally 'how much do you take'.
Long ii and long aa. The Jordanian dinar is in everyday use in the West Bank.

Form V verb, 3rd person masculine past, with ح as 7 and a doubled m. Palestinians use the ta- form (ta7ammast), not the Egyptian it- form. It is a Levantine-wide verb with no distinctively Palestinian replacement.
The existential fii is the normal Palestinian 'there is/are' and is not the preposition 'in' here.
This is a construct phrase, so the first ة is pronounced t. ق in 'a3de is a glottal stop, and the final ة after د is e. oDit 'a3de (أوضة قعدة) is also common.

The doubled y is written out (7ayyaak). الله is pronounced alla in connected speech. It is a somewhat Bedouin- or Gulf-flavoured welcome but is used in Palestinian; ahleen and yaa hala are the more neutral greetings.
mumkin + a subjunctive verb with the indirect object -li attached: tishra7li. The feminine form would be tishra7ili.
The verb tili3 'turned out' takes the feminine -it with syncope: Til3it. 'iSSa has a glottal ق and an emphatic doubled S. innu is 'that'. Som Palestinians say Tili3it instead.
The pronunciation is regular (ع shortened to 3a, ص as S). I am not sure this idiom is native to Palestinian; shadd/laa3ab a3Saabi and Tili3 3ala a3Saabi are the ones I know best.
biddi is the Palestinian 'I want'. a7kiilak has a long ii before -lak (to you, m.). ishi is the typically Palestinian 'something'.
The colloquial 'hundred' is miyye, with a doubled y and final e after ي. It is not MSA mi'a.
khubz and mil7 are both single-syllable with final clusters. 'And' is pronounced u after the consonant cluster. The idiom means a bond of shared hospitality.
Form V verb with a doubled j. It is understood and used, but a bit formal; in conversation istaghrab is the more usual 'be surprised'.
Passive participle of aHraj with the colloquial mi- prefix. ma7ruuj is also commonly said for 'embarrassed', while mu7rij means 'embarrassing'.
Taa marbuta after ي is e. The word is singular ('a curtain'; plural baraadi), and sitaara is an equally common synonym.
An MSA-origin noun that is genuinely used in speech about bookings and events. The final hamza is written as '.
Form X with a long ii: asta3iir. minnak has a doubled n. astalif is the everyday 'borrow' for money and small things; asta3iir is fine for books and objects.
maa 7ada is Palestinian 'nobody', with ما used as negation of the verb. biy3rif is the 3rd person present with the bi- prefix (also heard as bya3rif).
Construct phrase, so ة is pronounced t. il- assimilates to ص, giving iS-Saff. For a homeroom teacher Palestinian schools often say murabbiyit iS-Saff (مربّية الصف).
This is a slogan, so the verb keeps the formal ending -at, whereas plain colloquial would be 3aashit. filasTiin has an emphatic T and a long ii.
The Levantine month name is used in Palestine, often without the article (kaanuun awwal). Long uu in kaanuun and a doubled w in awwal.
